nodes.label: About the Editor-in-Chief
nodes.summary: Biographical note on Meyer R. Rosen, President of Interactive Consulting, Inc. and Editor-in-Chief of Harry's Cosmeticology 9th Ed. It lists his expertise in technical marketing, applied rheology, surface and interfacial chemistry, polymers and organosilicones, and his roles with the SCC, AIC and Euro Cosmetics Magazine.

nodes.label: Preface
nodes.summary: Editor's preface tracing Harry's Cosmeticology from Ralph Gordon Harry's 1954 first edition to the 9th edition, and the WWII military origins of modern cosmetics (sunscreens, flashburn creams, anti-sunburn lipsticks). It argues that population aging, genetics and epigenetics place the industry at a tipping point in the search for youth.

nodes.label: Marketing Concepts to Empower Technical People
nodes.summary: Explains the marketing concept: products should be developed only when a large enough group will buy them, so development is driven by market analysis. Covers situation/SWOT analysis, market segmentation, the Four P's, the new product-development process, types of innovation, patents and the need for cross-functional cooperation, noting 80-90% of new products fail.

nodes.label: Creating the Right Fragrance for Your Personal Care Product
nodes.summary: Guide to working with a fragrance house (perfumer-evaluator teams, library, QC) and to fragrance composition: natural and synthetic materials, top/middle/base notes, volatility, log Kow and odor thresholds. Also covers use-cycle evaluation, cost and carriers, troubleshooting color/stability/odor, EU 26 allergen labeling and fragrance types such as WS, WD, INCI blends, natural and GRAS fragrances.

nodes.label: Fragrance Packaging Design
nodes.summary: Describes fine-fragrance development as an integrated multi-sensory process aligning marketer, perfumer and designer via briefs. Uses consumer testing (e.g. Victoria's Secret Bombshell), color, bottle touch/ergonomics and storytelling as sensory cues so that packaging and scent avoid sensory dissonance.

nodes.label: Molecular Cell Biology and Gene Analysis for Cosmetics
nodes.summary: Introduces molecular cell biology for cosmetic chemists: proteins and amino acids, cell organelles, cell signaling and receptor classes, and epigenetics (DNA methylation, histone modification). Applies these to skin care via skin immunity, gene expression analysis and the Nrf2 and AMPK pathways activated by phytochemicals such as resveratrol and sulforaphane.

nodes.label: Society of Cosmetic Chemists
nodes.summary: U.S. professional society (SCC) of which the Editor-in-Chief is a member and serves as an advisor to its Advisory Committee.

nodes.label: Rheology
nodes.summary: Applied rheology, the study of flow and deformation of materials, listed among the Editor-in-Chief's areas of technical expertise.

nodes.label: Silicones
nodes.summary: Organosilicones, a polymer family listed among the editor's areas of expertise; silicones also mentioned as product bases with which fragrance carriers must be compatible.

nodes.label: Delivery Systems
nodes.summary: Technologies for delivering actives in personal care, the subject of Rosen's earlier Delivery System Handbook for Personal Care and Cosmetic Products.

nodes.label: Sunscreen
nodes.summary: Sun-screening agents were developed in WWII for men marooned on liferafts or in deserts facing severe solar exposure, a stimulus for cosmetic science.

nodes.label: Flashburn Cream
nodes.summary: WWII 'commando makeup' cream designed to protect exposed skin surfaces against burns.

nodes.label: Lipstick
nodes.summary: Anti-sunburn lipsticks were among the WWII military developments that stimulated cosmetic technology.

nodes.label: Barrier Cream
nodes.summary: Developed on the WWII home front, with special toilet soaps, to reduce dermatitis among workers.

nodes.label: Soap
nodes.summary: Soaps and special toilet soaps were developed for the military and home front in WWII, partly to reduce dermatitis.

nodes.label: Toothpaste
nodes.summary: Toothpastes were among products developed for the military in WWII.

nodes.label: Shaving Cream
nodes.summary: Shaving creams were among products developed for the military in WWII.

nodes.label: Dermatitis
nodes.summary: Skin inflammation that WWII home-front toilet soaps and barrier creams were developed to reduce.

nodes.label: Insect Repellents
nodes.summary: Ingredient class whose synthesis and development resulted from WWII-era cosmetic developments.

nodes.label: Emulsifiers
nodes.summary: Ingredient class developed further as a repercussion of WWII-era cosmetic developments.

nodes.label: Antioxidants
nodes.summary: Ingredients developed further after WWII; in molecular terms antioxidants cannot always fully neutralize ROS damage (Harman).

nodes.label: Preservatives
nodes.summary: Ingredient class whose development was stimulated by WWII-era cosmetic advances.

nodes.label: Surfactants
nodes.summary: Surface-active agents (detergents) developed after WWII; in fragrance work surfactants such as polysorbates solubilize or disperse hydrophobic fragrance oils in water.

nodes.label: Fragrance
nodes.summary: Complex, balanced mixture of natural and synthetic odorous materials (plus ~5-20% carrier) that covers base malodor, makes products appealing and reinforces product benefits; used in nearly every product type.

nodes.label: Cosmetic vs Drug Distinction
nodes.summary: Regulatory separation of cosmetics from drugs, which the editor argues masks a single underlying need to reverse the effects of gravity and time.

nodes.label: Epigenetics
nodes.summary: Somatically heritable states of gene expression resulting from changes in chromatin structure without altering DNA sequence; influenced by environmental factors and involved in inflammation, obesity, aging, immune disorders and cancer.

nodes.label: Skin Aging
nodes.summary: Age-related change in appearance that consumers seek to reverse; gene expression studies give insight into its mechanisms and DNA methylation plays a role in sun-exposed aging skin.

nodes.label: Genetics
nodes.summary: Breakthroughs in understanding the genetic code, cited with epigenetics and biochemistry as enabling approaches to look younger.

nodes.label: Marketing Concept
nodes.summary: Principle that no new products are developed unless it can be proven that a large enough group of people will buy them; product development is thus driven by marketing analysis rather than innovation.

nodes.label: Marketing Mix (Four P's)
nodes.summary: The 'Original Four' P's - Product, Price, Place and Promotion strategies - that form the foundation of the marketing program, tailored to market segments.

nodes.label: Product Strategy
nodes.summary: Foundation of marketing where marketing and R&D decide ingredients, positioning, packaging and branding before pricing; failed cooperation here often causes product failure.

nodes.label: Pricing Strategy
nodes.summary: Pricing must cover variable and fixed costs, consider competitor/substitute prices and willingness to pay; distributors take ~10% and retailers up to 50% of retail price.

nodes.label: Distribution Strategy (Place)
nodes.summary: Placement decisions choosing exclusive, selective or intensive distribution and retail channel mix, dependent on product and pricing strategies.

nodes.label: Promotion Strategy
nodes.summary: Marketing communication mix of advertising, PR, direct marketing, sales promotion and personal selling, combining push marketing to retailers and pull marketing to consumers.

nodes.label: SWOT Analysis
nodes.summary: Summary of a situation analysis into Strengths and Weaknesses (internal factors) and Opportunities and Threats (external factors) for decision-making and risk reduction.

nodes.label: Situation Analysis
nodes.summary: Objective analysis of internal controllable factors (mission, finance, IT, R&D, marketing) and external factors (industry, competition, economy, regulation) of the business environment; also called business analysis.

nodes.label: Market Segmentation
nodes.summary: Breaking a market into consumer segments sharing characteristics, combining demographics, psychographics and geographics, to tailor the marketing mix.

nodes.label: Market Research
nodes.summary: Surveys, focus groups and other methodologies used to assess consumer needs; intensive market research greatly reduces the marketer's risk.

nodes.label: Green Marketing Model
nodes.summary: Strategic marketing planning framework: internal analysis, external analysis, SWOT, objectives and budget, marketing strategy and program, and control and evaluation.

nodes.label: New Product-Development Process
nodes.summary: Seven-step process: idea generation, concept testing, business analysis/marketing planning, product development, market testing, commercialization and evaluation of market results.

nodes.label: Idea Generation
nodes.summary: First NPD step; ideas come from customers, competitors, employees, suppliers, universities, R&D and even other industries, often via brainstorming led by a technical marketing expert.

nodes.label: Concept Testing
nodes.summary: 'Proof of concept' testing in which relevant parties are interviewed, surveyed or join focus groups to prove a concept might work before further analysis.

nodes.label: Test Marketing
nodes.summary: Releasing a product in specific stores or regions before broad launch to reduce risk of failure; can tip off competitors and is little used in personal care.

nodes.label: Open Innovation
nodes.summary: Ideation process drawing ideas from outside the organization, e.g. hair care developers using carpet-industry fiber knowledge.

nodes.label: Stability Testing
nodes.summary: Testing of a formula (shelf-aging stability, rapid aging, freeze-thaw, light exposure) until results are satisfactory and the formula is robust under foreseeable conditions.

nodes.label: Microbial Contamination Testing
nodes.summary: Testing for bacterial contamination of a finalized prototype formula before commercialization.

nodes.label: Claim Substantiation
nodes.summary: Testing the finished product, even when actives are clinically tested, so that marketing claims can be substantiated.

nodes.label: Dusting
nodes.summary: Practice of including a non-efficacious amount of a story-driven ingredient, rendering the product ineffective; common in natural/organic and mainstream products.

nodes.label: FDA
nodes.summary: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, increasingly watching product claims and mandating elimination of false or misleading structure-function claims.

nodes.label: Structure-Function Claim
nodes.summary: Type of product claim the FDA has a mandate to keep from being false or misleading.

nodes.label: Innovation
nodes.summary: Determined by the degree of consumer behavioral change required, not novelty; most new products are continuous innovations and 'hot' ingredients are merely popular.

nodes.label: Continuous Innovation
nodes.summary: New product requiring almost no change in consumer behavior, e.g. a hand lotion with a new nonactive ingredient; most new products are of this type.

nodes.label: Dynamically Continuous Innovation
nodes.summary: Major change in a minor behavior or minor change in a major behavior, e.g. a hand lotion moving from jar to pump dispensing.

nodes.label: Discontinuous Innovation
nodes.summary: Disruptive innovation with an entirely new market application, e.g. hair regrowth or ingestible skin/hair supplements.

nodes.label: Patent
nodes.summary: U.S. patents require novelty, a non-obvious inventive step and industrial application and are exclusive for 20 years; author argues cosmetic patents are too easy to obtain.

nodes.label: Ingestible Beauty Supplement
nodes.summary: Skin and hair care products in the form of ingestible nutritional supplements, possibly the last true discontinuous innovation in the sector.

nodes.label: Hair Loss
nodes.summary: Concern addressed by hair regrowth, cited as an example of a new market application constituting discontinuous innovation.

nodes.label: Natural and Organic Ingredients
nodes.summary: Certified organic or natural ingredients chosen by marketing over synthetics, which can pose manufacturing constraints; this business has been plagued by dusting.

nodes.label: Packaging
nodes.summary: Labels, containers and applicators considered after formula finalization; an important part of the consumer experience and a key sensory cue in fragrance.

nodes.label: Push and Pull Marketing
nodes.summary: Push marketing encourages distributors and retailers to carry a product; pull marketing informs consumers about the product, claims and availability.

nodes.label: New Product Failure
nodes.summary: About 80-90% of new products fail to meet expectations and are deleted within a few years, often due to poor cross-functional cooperation and lack of market research.

nodes.label: Cross-Functional Collaboration
nodes.summary: Cooperation among marketing, R&D and manufacturing, dual-degree staff and employee training recommended to raise product success rates.

nodes.label: Hand Lotion
nodes.summary: Used as the example product for continuous (new nonactive ingredient) and dynamically continuous (jar to pump) innovation.

nodes.label: Fragrance House
nodes.summary: Company specializing solely in fragrance creation, with sales, evaluation, perfumery, applications, analytical, regulatory, marketing and QC departments and a library of tens of thousands of formulas.

nodes.label: Perfumer
nodes.summary: Specialist trained 5-10 years by apprenticeship who commits up to 3,000 raw materials to olfactive memory and composes fragrances, typically using 5-15 trials per new fragrance.

nodes.label: Fragrance Evaluator
nodes.summary: Translates the client's request into an olfactive structure, guides perfumers on trends and impartially critiques creations; likened to a food critic or golf caddy and represents the marketer.

nodes.label: Fragrance Library
nodes.summary: A fragrance house's collection of completed, approved but unsold formulas (tens of thousands) used for future requests; chosen formulas are removed once purchased.

nodes.label: Triangle Test
nodes.summary: Sensory discrimination test in which panelists identify the odd sample among three (two control, one test or vice versa); used by fragrance QC to compare production to standard.

nodes.label: Fragrance Quality Control
nodes.summary: QC compares production batches to a standard by triangle test plus flash point, refractive index, specific gravity and color specifications.

nodes.label: RIFM
nodes.summary: Research Institute for Fragrance Materials; conducts safety and environmental studies on fragrance raw materials and maintains the master list of permitted materials.

nodes.label: IFRA
nodes.summary: International Fragrance Association; regulates the amount of each fragrance material usable in 11 product categories via the QRA document and educates the public.

nodes.label: Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA)
nodes.summary: IFRA document delineating maximum use levels of fragrance materials per product category (11 categories from lip care to candles) based on expected exposure.

nodes.label: Essential Oils
nodes.summary: Natural fragrance materials usually obtained by steam distillation (citrus by peel expression); used at ~1-20% in standard fragrances, adding naturalness and complexity but cost volatility.

nodes.label: Concretes
nodes.summary: Natural extracts obtained by hydrophobic-solvent extraction of plants, containing essential oil plus waxes; very expensive touch ingredients.

nodes.label: Absolutes
nodes.summary: Ethanol extract of a concrete with waxes removed (or supercritical CO2 extract); used as touch ingredients at 0.001-0.100% for rich odor value.

nodes.label: Natural Isolates
nodes.summary: Single components removed from essential oils by crystallization or fractional distillation without chemical transformation, e.g. menthol from peppermint oil.

nodes.label: Synthetic Fragrance Materials
nodes.summary: Fragrance materials made by chemical reaction (from crude sulfate turpentine, petroleum or plant molecules); the majority of materials, well characterized, plentiful, cost-stable and not seasonal.

nodes.label: Steam Distillation
nodes.summary: Usual method of obtaining essential oils; the oil floats on the distillate water and is separated and dried.

nodes.label: Fractional Distillation
nodes.summary: Distillation of an essential oil separating components by differing boiling points to obtain natural isolates.

nodes.label: Supercritical CO2 Extraction
nodes.summary: Extraction of plants with supercritical carbon dioxide yielding absolutes of extremely faithful odor quality.

nodes.label: Solvent Extraction
nodes.summary: Extraction of plant material with a hydrophobic solvent (yielding a concrete) or ethanol (yielding an absolute).

nodes.label: Menthol
nodes.summary: Natural isolate obtained by crystallizing it out of peppermint oil.

nodes.label: Peppermint Oil
nodes.summary: Essential oil from which menthol is crystallized as a natural isolate.

nodes.label: Citrus Oils
nodes.summary: Essential oils obtained by squeezing fruit peels, a byproduct of the citrus food industry and therefore relatively inexpensive; supply affected by weather disasters.

nodes.label: Crude Sulfate Turpentine
nodes.summary: Feedstock from which many synthetic fragrance materials are derived.

nodes.label: Botanical Extracts
nodes.summary: Plant materials used for marketing or performance rather than odor, from any plant part and solvent; labeled per PCPC nomenclature.

nodes.label: Personal Care Products Council
nodes.summary: U.S. trade association (formerly CTFA) that assigns INCI names and governs botanical and ingredient label naming.

nodes.label: INCI Nomenclature
nodes.summary: International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients names listed by the PCPC, used for ingredient labels; INCI fragrance blends list each material instead of 'fragrance'.

nodes.label: Fragrance Note (Accord)
nodes.summary: A note or accord is an odor character, almost a mini-fragrance, composed of about 2-20 materials each contributing a facet; fragrances combine several accords.

nodes.label: Fragrance Pyramid
nodes.summary: Industry-standard diagram representing a fragrance's top, middle and base note characters.

nodes.label: Top Notes
nodes.summary: Immediately perceivable, most volatile notes such as citrus, green, marine, ozone and light fruity characters.

nodes.label: Middle Notes
nodes.summary: The 'coeur' (heart), the most characteristic part of a fragrance: florals, sweet, gourmand, deeper fruity and lighter woody notes.

nodes.label: Base Notes
nodes.summary: Longest-lasting, least volatile and most expensive notes (musks, woods, amber, heavy florals) that support and round a fragrance.

nodes.label: Volatility
nodes.summary: Ease of vaporizing a fragrance component, indicated by boiling point and vapor pressure; green, citrus and light fruity notes are most volatile, musks and woods least.

nodes.label: Octanol-Water Partition Coefficient
nodes.summary: log Kow index of a material's partitioning between octanol and water; each unit means ~1,000x (as stated) more material prefers the oily phase; most fragrance materials are hydrophobic.

nodes.label: Raoult's Law
nodes.summary: Principle cited for how a component's volatility changes from the neat state due to solubility in or interaction with a product matrix.

nodes.label: Odor Detection Threshold
nodes.summary: Minimum air concentration at which a material becomes perceivable; food and decay odors have low thresholds, survival-neutral florals and woods higher ones.

nodes.label: Anosmia
nodes.summary: Inability to smell a specific material regardless of concentration, often genetic for certain musks or sandalwood; total anosmia is rare and usually from injury or medication.

nodes.label: Olfactory Saturation
nodes.summary: Temporary, reversible blocking of odor receptors after smelling a strong material at high concentration.

nodes.label: Olfactory Adaptation
nodes.summary: Brain ceases to recognize an odor smelled continuously, e.g. after minutes in a zoo monkey house.

nodes.label: Trigeminal Response
nodes.summary: Separate neurological pathway triggered by odorants like ammonia, making such odors nearly impossible to neutralize with fragrance alone.

nodes.label: Ammonia
nodes.summary: Highly volatile gas with odor and trigeminal response; at hair-color concentrations fragrance can barely mask it.

nodes.label: Bisulfites
nodes.summary: Ingredients releasing sulfur dioxide odor; usually at low enough levels that fragrance can mitigate the smell.

nodes.label: Malodor Masking
nodes.summary: Fragrance's role of covering the base odor of a product; limited for highly volatile gases with higher vapor pressure than fragrance materials.

nodes.label: Product-Use Cycle
nodes.summary: Sequence of consumer evaluation points from point of purchase through dispensing, bloom with water, rinse, drying or leave-on wear; usually one key evaluation point dominates.

nodes.label: Fragrance Bloom
nodes.summary: Burst of fragrance when water is added to a rinse-off product, often the key evaluation point for rinse-off categories.

nodes.label: Rinse-Off Product
nodes.summary: Product category (e.g. shampoo, body wash) evaluated at bloom, rinse and dry stages; bloom is usually the key evaluation point.

nodes.label: Leave-On Product
nodes.summary: Products such as lotions and hair gels whose key fragrance evaluation is at application and over the effectiveness time frame.

nodes.label: Fragrance Carriers
nodes.summary: Odorless solvents (~5-20% of a fragrance) needed for physical stability or as processing aids; must match the product base solubility.

nodes.label: Dipropylene Glycol
nodes.summary: Common fragrance carrier with the most water solubility of common carriers; poorly soluble in bath oils and silicones, forming a second phase in bath oil.

nodes.label: Isopropyl Myristate
nodes.summary: Very hydrophobic fragrance carrier that works in oils and silicones and yields homogeneous bath oil, but may not suit sulfate-free shampoo.

nodes.label: Diethyl Phthalate
nodes.summary: Very good carrier for all product types, but many consumer-product companies no longer allow its use.

nodes.label: Benzyl Benzoate
nodes.summary: One of the most common fragrance carriers.

nodes.label: Triethyl Citrate
nodes.summary: One of the most common fragrance carriers.

nodes.label: Polysorbate 20
nodes.summary: Common fragrance carrier and polysorbate surfactant used to pre-solubilize fragrance oils in water-soluble fragrances.

nodes.label: Hydrogenated Soybean Oil
nodes.summary: Highly hydrophobic cost-reducing carrier for natural INCI fragrance blends.

nodes.label: Medium-Chain Triglycerides
nodes.summary: Medium-chain vegetable triglycerides used as inexpensive stable carrier oils for natural INCI blends.

nodes.label: Chelating Agents
nodes.summary: Adding a chelating agent and keeping the product slightly acidic can help prevent fragrance-induced color change.

nodes.label: Pearlizers
nodes.summary: Pearlescent agents that may separate on heating in fragranced products, a sign of phase instability.

nodes.label: Product Discoloration
nodes.summary: Fragrance-induced color shift: vanilla/spun-sugar gourmand notes turn products yellow or pink; grapey, jasmine or tuberose notes turn them pink.

nodes.label: Phase Separation
nodes.summary: Physical instability where a product splits into layers (e.g. freeze-thaw) or pearlizers separate; may be solved by changing fragrance carrier.

nodes.label: Odor Instability
nodes.summary: Fragrance fading or 'turning' to unpleasant odor during stability testing, possibly from reaction with the base or actives.

nodes.label: Freeze-Thaw Testing
nodes.summary: Stability test cycling temperature that can reveal phase separation into distinct layers.

nodes.label: Traditional Fragrance
nodes.summary: Standard mixture of natural and synthetic materials with 5-20% carrier labeled as 'fragrance'; most common, versatile and cost-stable, and the default supplied.

nodes.label: EU Allergen-Label-Free Fragrance
nodes.summary: Fragrance containing none of the 26 EU-labeled allergens above thresholds; excludes natural essential oils, limiting the perfumer's palette.

nodes.label: EU 26 Fragrance Allergens
nodes.summary: EU mandate, based on SCCNFP opinion, that any of 26 dermal allergens present above set levels in a finished product be listed on the ingredient label.

nodes.label: SCCNFP
nodes.summary: EU Scientific Committee on Cosmetic Products and Non-Food Products whose consensus identified up to 26 fragrance dermal allergens.
aliases: Scientific Committee on Cosmetic Products and Non-Food Products

nodes.label: European Union
nodes.summary: Market requiring labeling of 26 fragrance allergens above threshold levels on cosmetic ingredient labels.

nodes.label: Contact Allergy
nodes.summary: Dermal allergy to fragrance substances; up to 26 fragrance materials are identified as dermal allergens.

nodes.label: Water-Soluble Fragrance
nodes.summary: 'WS' fragrance pre-solubilized in surfactant (typically 70-80% polysorbate) for clear water-based products like hair gel; only 20-30% provides odor.

nodes.label: Water-Dispersible Fragrance
nodes.summary: 'WD' fragrance with ~30-50% surfactant forming a hazy semi-stable dispersion, used for accurate low-level dosing such as facial wipes.

nodes.label: INCI Fragrance Blend
nodes.summary: Fragrance in which every material has a PCPC INCI name so the label lists ingredients instead of 'fragrance'; types are natural, allergen-label-free, traditional and unscented.

nodes.label: Unscented INCI Blend
nodes.summary: Simple blend of 2-3 neutral-smelling INCI materials that mitigates base odor without adding a recognizable fragrance, e.g. for eye or facial cream.

nodes.label: Natural Fragrance
nodes.summary: Fragrance of essential oils, absolutes, concretes, isolates and fermentation products; 3-10 times more expensive than traditional fragrances with limited odor characters.

nodes.label: Essential Oil Blend
nodes.summary: Most limited, most expensive natural fragrance using only whole essential oils (citrus, herbal, lavender, woody, few florals), with seasonal price swings.

nodes.label: GRAS Fragrance
nodes.summary: Niche fragrance where each material has a FEMA-GRAS number or is a recognized flavor, for lip balms, products entering the mouth and children's toys; typically fruity and simple.

nodes.label: FEMA GRAS
nodes.summary: Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association 'Generally Recognized as Safe' flavor designation required for each material in GRAS fragrances.

nodes.label: Fragrance Concentration-Cost Principle
nodes.summary: Buying concentrated fragrance is most cost-effective: a $40/kg fragrance at 0.5% costs $0.20/kg product, while a diluted $20/kg version needs 1.3% costing $0.26/kg.

nodes.label: Solubilization
nodes.summary: Using surfactant to solubilize hydrophobic fragrance oil in water; start at 2-3 parts surfactant to 1 part oil, up to 4-5 parts for clarity.

nodes.label: Polysorbates
nodes.summary: Affordable surfactants used as diluent/compatibilizer in water-soluble fragrances.

nodes.label: Oil-in-Water Emulsion
nodes.summary: Product base type, e.g. facial creme, into which fragrances must be adapted.

nodes.label: Micellar Solution
nodes.summary: Surfactant-based product base such as shampoo or body wash in which fragrance perception differs from the neat oil.

nodes.label: Shampoo
nodes.summary: Rinse-off micellar product; fragrance is most concentrated in bottle and on hands, then dilutes below detection thresholds as water is added.

nodes.label: Body Wash
nodes.summary: Micellar rinse-off product base for fragrance.

nodes.label: Hair Gel
nodes.summary: Water-based styling product requiring water-soluble fragrance for clarity; key fragrance point is application.

nodes.label: Bath Oil
nodes.summary: Solution of fragrance in oils; dipropylene glycol carrier forms a second phase whereas isopropyl myristate stays homogeneous.

nodes.label: Facial Wipe
nodes.summary: Product fragranced at very low level (e.g. 0.010%) using water-dispersible fragrance diluted in water.

nodes.label: Lip Balm
nodes.summary: Product that may enter the mouth and so requires GRAS fragrances.

nodes.label: Hair Color
nodes.summary: Product containing ammonia at levels whose odor fragrance can only slightly mitigate.

nodes.label: Body Lotion
nodes.summary: Leave-on product where fragrance hours after application may reassure consumers that moisturizing continues; mass-market body creams use higher fragrance intensity than high-end facial creams.

nodes.label: Fine Fragrance
nodes.summary: Perfume product where every moment from application to wash-off is a key evaluation point; over 1,000 launched globally in 2011.

nodes.label: Fragrance Packaging Design
nodes.summary: Integrated design of bottle, carton, color and name aligned with scent and story so sensory cues communicate the olfactive character and emotional concept.

nodes.label: Product Brief
nodes.summary: Document led by Brand Development/Marketing outlining objective and strategy (brand identity, target consumer, positioning, pricing, distribution, ship date); refined into fragrance and creative briefs.

nodes.label: Fragrance Brief
nodes.summary: Brief to the fragrance house with brand overview, psychographic target, olfactive story and mood board, olfactive category, oil cost target, benchmarks, regulatory needs and timeline.

nodes.label: Mood Board
nodes.summary: Visual collage in the fragrance brief conveying olfactive story, color direction and product personality to the perfumer.

nodes.label: Olfactive Families
nodes.summary: Fragrance categories: primary citrus, floral, fougere, woody, chypre, oriental; secondary include marine, aldehydic, aromatic, green, spicy, fruity, musky, gourmand, leather/animalic.

nodes.label: Sensory Cues
nodes.summary: Cues through bottle, packaging, color and scent that set consumer expectations and communicate olfactive character and emotional story.

nodes.label: Sensory Dissonance
nodes.summary: Consumer confusion experienced when bottle, packaging, color story and scent are not aligned.

nodes.label: Consumer Testing
nodes.summary: Hybrid qualitative (field tests, shop-alongs, in-home visits, diaries, focus groups, interviews, in-store intercepts) and quantitative (surveys) testing guiding development.

nodes.label: Blind Fragrance Test
nodes.summary: Consumers smell a fragrance on skin, on a blotter, then completely blind without sensory cues to assess purchase intent and descriptors.

nodes.label: Color-Scent Association
nodes.summary: Color is perhaps the strongest cue aligning expectations: blue-calm/watery/ozonic, green-fresh/nature, red-sexy/powerful, purple-luxury/mystery.

nodes.label: Flanker
nodes.summary: Fragrance variation of an original, distinguished by color to communicate newness and extend brand lifecycle (e.g. Marc Jacobs Daisy versions).

nodes.label: Bottle Ergonomics
nodes.summary: Designing bottle shape, weight and cap for emotional and functional feel, e.g. a tapered, dumbbell-weighted men's sport bottle with spray-through cap.

nodes.label: Fragrance Storytelling
nodes.summary: Conveying a sensory story visually and verbally in the brief to stimulate the perfumer, then releasing it to consumers through all sensory cues.

nodes.label: Victoria's Secret
nodes.summary: Retailer whose fragrance head Mark Knitowski tests scents with consumers across 1,000+ stores; its 'Bombshell' fragrance, relaunched from 'Signature', won awards in 2011.

nodes.label: Coty
nodes.summary: Fragrance company (SVP Catherine Walsh) behind celebrity and designer brands including Marc Jacobs Dot; uses consumer testing to lead trends.

nodes.label: Sensory Spectrum Inc.
nodes.summary: Sensory evaluation firm led by Gail Vance Civille, advocating consumer involvement in preliminary concept work.

nodes.label: Human Genome Project
nodes.summary: Project that revolutionized molecular biology research; many current techniques and gene-interaction knowledge derive from it.

nodes.label: Molecular Cell Biology
nodes.summary: Field investigating how cells develop, operate, communicate and control their activities, increasingly relevant to formulation chemists.

nodes.label: DNA
nodes.summary: Deoxyribonucleic acid; the hereditary storage form of genetic information whose genes indirectly control protein synthesis.

nodes.label: RNA
nodes.summary: Ribonucleic acid that transfers information within the cell and provides the template for protein synthesis.

nodes.label: Messenger RNA
nodes.summary: RNA type coding the chemical blueprint for a protein during synthesis.

nodes.label: Proteins
nodes.summary: Working molecules of the cell built from 20 amino acids; mammalian cells contain up to 10,000 kinds whose 3D structure determines function.

nodes.label: Amino Acids
nodes.summary: Twenty building blocks of proteins classified by side-chain polarity; arginine, lysine, aspartate and glutamate dominate protein charge.

nodes.label: Histidine
nodes.summary: Amino acid with pKa 6.8 (cytoplasmic pH); protonation of its side chain modulates activity of numerous proteins.

nodes.label: Cysteine
nodes.summary: Amino acid whose reactive sulfhydryl oxidizes to form disulfide bonds that maintain folded extracellular proteins.

nodes.label: Glycine
nodes.summary: Smallest amino acid (single hydrogen R group) fitting tight spaces; with proline found where the chain loops back.

nodes.label: Proline
nodes.summary: Amino acid found with glycine at protein-surface loop locations.

nodes.label: Arginine
nodes.summary: Amino acid positively charged at neutral pH, a major contributor to protein charge.

nodes.label: Lysine
nodes.summary: Amino acid positively charged at neutral pH, a major contributor to protein charge.

nodes.label: Disulfide Bond
nodes.summary: Covalent S-S bond formed by oxidation of two cysteine sulfhydryls, common in extracellular proteins to maintain folded structure.

nodes.label: Cell
nodes.summary: Membrane-bound unit containing DNA and cytoplasm; eukaryotic cells contain organelles and vesicles.

nodes.label: Plasma Membrane
nodes.summary: Membrane enclosing each cell containing receptor and transport proteins that let the cell interact with its environment.

nodes.label: Nucleus
nodes.summary: Largest organelle and control center of the eukaryotic cell, repository of genetic information; contains the nucleolus and nuclear pores.

nodes.label: Endoplasmic Reticulum
nodes.summary: Largest internal membrane, a lipid bilayer studded with ribosomes (rough ER) where proteins with signal sequences are synthesized.

nodes.label: Golgi Apparatus
nodes.summary: Vesicle-forming system that receives proteins from the ER for release outside the cell.

nodes.label: Lysosome
nodes.summary: Membrane-bound digestive vesicle containing acid hydrolases that break down proteins and debris.

nodes.label: Peroxisome
nodes.summary: Vesicle containing catalase and oxidative enzymes that breaks down toxic hydrogen peroxide and digests fatty acids.

nodes.label: Mitochondria
nodes.summary: Organelles with their own DNA that carry out the cell's oxidative metabolism.

nodes.label: Ribosome
nodes.summary: Framework for protein synthesis, with subunits made in the nucleolus.

nodes.label: Chromatin
nodes.summary: DNA-protein material of eukaryotic chromosomes organized into nucleosomes; its winding plays a role in gene regulation.

nodes.label: Histones
nodes.summary: Alkaline nuclear proteins that package DNA into nucleosomes; their modifications regulate transcription, repair and replication.

nodes.label: Nucleosome
nodes.summary: Repeating unit of chromatin in which DNA coils around histones, resembling a bead on a string.

nodes.label: Catalase
nodes.summary: Peroxisomal enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Peroxide
nodes.summary: Molecule toxic when it builds up in cells; H2O2-induced premature senescence of keratinocytes was prevented by AMPK activation with resveratrol.

nodes.label: Cell Signaling
nodes.summary: Communication via ligands binding receptors in three stages: reception, transduction and response; signals are endocrine, paracrine or autocrine.

nodes.label: Cell-Surface Receptors
nodes.summary: Four major classes: enzyme-linked receptors, G-protein-coupled receptors, ion-channel receptors and tyrosine kinase-linked receptors.

nodes.label: G-Protein-Coupled Receptor
nodes.summary: Receptor that activates or inhibits an enzyme generating a second messenger or modulates an ion channel.

nodes.label: Ion Channels
nodes.summary: Membrane components letting ions pass; ion-channel receptors change conformation to alter membrane potential.

nodes.label: Protein Kinases
nodes.summary: Enzymes that phosphorylate proteins on tyrosine or serine/threonine, activated by signaling pathways.

nodes.label: GTPase
nodes.summary: Proteins acting as molecular switches turning cell signaling on or off.

nodes.label: Epidermal Growth Factor
nodes.summary: Protein hormone that signals adjacent cells when membrane-bound and acts as an endocrine signal after protease cleavage.

nodes.label: DNA Methylation
nodes.summary: Addition of a methyl group to cytosine (or adenine) that alters gene expression; promoters become hypermethylated with age and it plays a role in sun-exposed aging skin.

nodes.label: Histone Modification
nodes.summary: Acetylation, phosphorylation, methylation and ubiquitination of histones that alter chromatin structure and regulate transcription; acetylation relaxes chromatin, raising transcription.

nodes.label: Gene Expression
nodes.summary: Conversion of gene information into mRNA and then protein; how cells make the right proteins at the right time and quantity.

nodes.label: Transcription
nodes.summary: First step of gene expression in which DNA is copied into RNA by RNA polymerase.

nodes.label: Translation
nodes.summary: Ribosomal processing of mRNA into a chain of amino acids forming proteins.

nodes.label: RNA Polymerase
nodes.summary: Enzyme that makes RNA copies of DNA once chromosomes uncoil.

nodes.label: Transcription Factors
nodes.summary: DNA-binding proteins that switch genes on or off by promoting or blocking transcription; mutations are linked to diabetes, autoimmunity and cancer.

nodes.label: Cytokines
nodes.summary: Signaling molecules regulating growth, differentiation, migration, immunity and inflammation; malfunction leads to arthritis, cardiac disease and cancer.

nodes.label: Interferons
nodes.summary: Cytokine glycoproteins released in response to pathogens or tumor cells that activate immune defenses and interfere with viral replication.

nodes.label: Inflammasome
nodes.summary: Large intracellular multiprotein complex central to innate immunity; UV radiation activates inflammasomes in keratinocytes.

nodes.label: Keratinocyte
nodes.summary: Epidermal cell acting as a sensor of danger from pathogens, irritants and toxins; UV activates its inflammasomes.

nodes.label: Langerhans Cell
nodes.summary: Immune cell present in the epidermis contributing to skin immune homeostasis.

nodes.label: Mast Cell
nodes.summary: Immune cell found in the epidermis and dermis.

nodes.label: Macrophage
nodes.summary: Immune cell found in skin; activated by interferons.

nodes.label: T-Cell
nodes.summary: Lymphocyte present in skin; interferons increase antigen presentation to T-lymphocytes.

nodes.label: Dermis
nodes.summary: Skin layer drained by lymphatic and vascular conduits through which immune cells traffic.

nodes.label: Epidermis
nodes.summary: Outer skin layer containing keratinocytes, Langerhans cells, T-cells and other immune cells.

nodes.label: Skin Immunity
nodes.summary: Coordinated immune response by keratinocytes and skin-resident immune cells to barrier disruption (UV, trauma, irritants, infection) to maintain homeostasis.

nodes.label: Homeostasis
nodes.summary: Equilibrium of the internal environment; disturbances decrease cell and organism function.

nodes.label: UV Radiation
nodes.summary: Ultraviolet light activates keratinocyte inflammasomes and inflammatory pathways and is a form of barrier disruption.

nodes.label: UVA Radiation
nodes.summary: Ultraviolet A irradiation from which Nrf2 protects keratinocytes.

nodes.label: Inflammation
nodes.summary: Immune process mediated by cytokines; epigenetic changes are involved and Nrf2 signals protection against it.

nodes.label: Nrf2 Signaling Pathway
nodes.summary: Stress-sensing transcription factor and master cytoprotective regulator activating >200 genes for detoxification and protection against oxidative stress and inflammation; interacts with p53 and NF-kB.

nodes.label: AMPK
nodes.summary: AMP-activated protein kinase, a three-protein master metabolic sensor regulating cellular energy homeostasis, lipid and glucose metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis; intersects mTOR, ERK, p53 and ATM pathways.

nodes.label: p53
nodes.summary: Tumor suppressor protein encoded by TP53, 'guardian of the genome', regulating the cell cycle; interacts with Nrf2 and AMPK.

nodes.label: NF-kB
nodes.summary: Nuclear factor kappa B, a key cell regulator interacting with Nrf2 in age-related disease.

nodes.label: mTOR
nodes.summary: Serine/threonine kinase (mammalian target of rapamycin) controlling cell division and survival; part of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway intersecting AMPK.

nodes.label: MAPK/ERK Pathway
nodes.summary: Protein chain relaying a signal from a surface receptor to nuclear DNA via phosphorylation; involved in tumor formation and cell growth.

nodes.label: RAS
nodes.summary: Low-molecular-weight G-protein binding GTP/GDP, part of the Ras/PI3K/mTOR growth pathway.

nodes.label: Reactive Oxygen Species
nodes.summary: Molecules that Harman (1956) proposed cause indiscriminate oxidative damage not always neutralized by antioxidants; Nrf2 protects against ROS damage.

nodes.label: Oxidative Stress
nodes.summary: Cellular stress from oxidation; Nrf2 signals protection against it, though it is one factor of multifactorial stress resistance.

nodes.label: Free Radical Theory of Aging
nodes.summary: Harman's 1956 theory that ROS cause cumulative oxidative damage driving aging; recent data, e.g. long-lived species with high oxidative damage, question its validity.

nodes.label: Cellular Stress Resistance
nodes.summary: Emerging theory that longevity tracks resistance to multiple nonoxidative stressors (heat, heavy metals, xenobiotics), coordinated by Nrf2.

nodes.label: Cellular Senescence
nodes.summary: Cellular aging state linked with aging and cancer; H2O2-induced premature keratinocyte senescence was prevented by resveratrol via AMPK.

nodes.label: Oxidative Metabolism
nodes.summary: Cellular respiration in mitochondria converting glucose and oxygen into CO2, water and energy stored as ATP.

nodes.label: ATP
nodes.summary: Adenosine triphosphate, the chemical energy store common to all organisms.

nodes.label: Molecular Chaperones
nodes.summary: Protein families that stabilize, unfold or assist folding of proteins; part of the cytoprotective stress pathway.

nodes.label: Xenobiotics
nodes.summary: Chemicals foreign to an organism (drugs, pollutants); among the stressors against which cellular resistance exists.

nodes.label: Sulforaphane
nodes.summary: Broccoli component found effective via the Nrf2 pathway.

nodes.label: Quercetin
nodes.summary: Polyphenolic associated with Nrf2 activation; protects keratinocytes from UVA via Nrf2.

nodes.label: Resveratrol
nodes.summary: Polyphenol associated with Nrf2 activation that activates AMPK and prevented H2O2-induced premature senescence in human keratinocyte cultures.

nodes.label: Caffeic Acid
nodes.summary: Polyphenolic component associated with Nrf2 activation.

nodes.label: Epicatechin
nodes.summary: Catechin polyphenol associated with Nrf2 activation.

nodes.label: Epigallocatechin Gallate
nodes.summary: Green tea catechin associated with Nrf2 activation and reported to activate AMPK.

nodes.label: Catechin
nodes.summary: Polyphenolic component associated with Nrf2 activation.

nodes.label: Curcumin
nodes.summary: Plant-derived compound reported to activate AMPK.

nodes.label: Garlic Oil
nodes.summary: Food-derived material reported to activate AMPK.

nodes.label: Berberine
nodes.summary: Plant alkaloid (traditional medicine) reported to activate AMPK.

nodes.label: Polyphenols
nodes.summary: Phytochemical class including quercetin, resveratrol, caffeic acid and catechins, associated with Nrf2 activation.

nodes.label: Green Tea
nodes.summary: Source of epigallocatechin-3-gallate, an AMPK activator.

nodes.label: Gene Expression Analysis
nodes.summary: Study of genes, their protein products and regulatory networks; bioactive ingredients' effects can be detected via molecular assays using known markers.

nodes.label: Biological Markers
nodes.summary: Identifiable substances, genes or characteristics indicating disease or abnormality; changes in gene and protein expression are the markers measured.

nodes.label: Epigenetic Therapy
nodes.summary: Anticipated skin-care approach to improve aging skin appearance by targeting epigenetic changes in hydration, barrier repair, ECM renewal, pigmentation and antioxidant capacity.

nodes.label: Extracellular Matrix
nodes.summary: Dermal matrix whose renewal is a skin-care target of epigenetic studies.

nodes.label: Skin Barrier
nodes.summary: Skin's primary interface and first line of defense against pathogens and insults; barrier repair is an epigenetic study target.

nodes.label: Skin Hydration
nodes.summary: Moisture state of skin, a target of gene expression and epigenetic studies.

nodes.label: Skin Pigmentation
nodes.summary: Pigmentation process examined in epigenetic skin-care studies.

nodes.label: Cancer
nodes.summary: Disease linked to epigenetic changes, DNA methylation, transcription factor mutations and cytokine malfunction; actives may prevent or, after onset, sometimes worsen malignancy.

nodes.label: Chromosome
nodes.summary: Linear DNA units of eukaryotes associated with histones and extended as chromatin.
